title: Standard Deviation
definition: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and indicates the typical amount by which individual data points differ from the mean; it is widely used to assess the risk or volatility of investment returns.
example: A mutual fund with higher standard deviation of returns is considered more volatile than one with a lower standard deviation.

title: Cost of Equity
definition: The cost of equity is the return a company must offer investors to compensate for the risk of holding its equity. It reflects the opportunity cost for shareholders and is used in calculating the weighted average cost of capital.
example: If a firm has a beta of 1.2, a risk-free rate of 3%, and a market risk premium of 6%, its cost of equity under CAPM is 3% + 1.2×6% = 10.2%.

title: Cost of Debt
definition: The cost of debt is the effective rate a company pays on its borrowed funds, adjusted for tax benefits. It measures the cost of raising capital through debt financing.
example: A company with a 5% interest rate on its bonds and a 21% tax rate has an after-tax cost of debt of 5% × (1 – 0.21) = 3.95%.

title: Capital Rationing
definition: Capital rationing is a situation in which a company restricts its investment in new projects despite having positive net present value projects, due to limited funds or risk considerations.
example: A firm with a $10 million budget only funds the top two of five viable projects, even though all projects have positive NPVs.

title: Retention Ratio
definition: The retention ratio, or plowback ratio, represents the proportion of earnings a company retains for reinvestment rather than paying out as dividends. It equals one minus the dividend payout ratio.
example: If a company earns $100 million and distributes $30 million in dividends, the retention ratio is 70%.

title: Dividend Cover Ratio
definition: The dividend cover ratio (dividend coverage ratio) measures how many times a company’s net income can cover its dividend payments. It is calculated as earnings per share divided by dividends per share.
example: A firm with earnings per share of $2 and dividends per share of $0.50 has a dividend cover ratio of 4.

title: Debt-to-EBITDA Ratio
definition: The debt-to-EBITDA ratio gauges a company’s ability to pay off its debt using earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA). It is found by dividing total debt by EBITDA.
example: A company with total debt of $400 million and EBITDA of $100 million has a debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 4.

title: Asset Turnover Ratio
definition: The asset turnover ratio measures how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate revenue. It is calculated by dividing net sales by average total assets.
example: If a firm generates $2 million in sales with average assets of $1 million, its asset turnover ratio is 2.

title: Fixed Asset Turnover Ratio
definition: The fixed asset turnover ratio evaluates how well a company uses its fixed assets to generate sales. It equals net sales divided by net fixed assets.
example: A business with net sales of $1.5 million and net fixed assets of $0.5 million has a fixed asset turnover ratio of 3.

title: Operating Leverage
definition: Operating leverage measures how sensitive a company’s operating income is to changes in sales due to fixed costs in its cost structure. High operating leverage means small changes in sales result in large changes in operating profit.
example: A software firm with high fixed development costs and low variable costs exhibits high operating leverage.

title: Financial Leverage
definition: Financial leverage refers to the use of borrowed funds to amplify returns on investment. While leverage can increase returns, it also heightens the risk of losses if earnings do not cover debt obligations.
example: A company funded 70% by debt and 30% by equity has high financial leverage.

title: Cash Flow from Operations (CFO)
definition: Cash flow from operations represents cash generated or used by a company’s core business activities. It is the first section of the cash flow statement and indicates whether a firm’s operating cash can sustain its operations.
example: A retail chain collects $500 K from customers and pays $300 K to suppliers and employees, resulting in operating cash flow of $200 K.

title: Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF)
definition: Free cash flow to firm is the cash available to all investors, including debt and equity holders, after covering operating expenses, taxes, capital expenditures, and working capital requirements.
example: A firm with EBIT of $100 M, tax rate 30%, depreciation $20 M, capital expenditures $40 M, and a $10 M increase in working capital generates FCFF = 100*(1-0.3) + 20 – 40 – 10 = $50 M.

title: Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE)
definition: Free cash flow to equity is cash available to equity shareholders after accounting for operating expenses, capital expenditures, changes in working capital, debt repayments, and new borrowing.
example: A company with net income of $80 M, depreciation of $15 M, capital expenditures of $30 M, a $5 M increase in working capital, and net borrowing of $10 M has FCFE of 80 + 15 – 30 – 5 + 10 = $70 M.

title: Days Payable Outstanding (DPO)
definition: Days payable outstanding measures the average number of days a company takes to pay its suppliers. It is calculated as (accounts payable ÷ cost of goods sold) × 365.
example: If accounts payable are $100 K and cost of goods sold is $1.2 M, the DPO is (100,000 ÷ 1,200,000) × 365 ≈ 30.4 days.

title: Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
definition: Gross domestic product is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country’s borders during a specific period. It is a key measure of economic output and growth.
example: In 2023, the United States’ GDP was roughly $26 trillion, reflecting the combined value of goods and services produced.

title: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
definition: The consumer price index measures the average change over time in the prices paid by consumers for a basket of goods and services. It is used to monitor inflation.
example: If the CPI rises from 200 to 204 in a year, the annual inflation rate is (204 – 200) / 200 = 2%.

title: Producer Price Index (PPI)
definition: The producer price index tracks the average change in prices received by domestic producers for their output. It provides insight into inflation from the producers’ perspective.
example: An increase of 3% in the PPI for manufacturing signals that producers are receiving higher prices for their goods.

title: Unemployment Rate
definition: The unemployment rate is the percentage of the labor force that is unemployed and actively seeking work. It reflects the health of a country’s labor market.
example: If 5 million people are unemployed out of a labor force of 100 million, the unemployment rate is 5%.

title: Interest Rate Risk
definition: Interest rate risk is the risk that changes in interest rates will negatively affect the value of investments, particularly bonds. When interest rates rise, bond prices typically fall.
example: Bond portfolios lose value when market interest rates rise because existing bonds with lower coupons become less attractive.

title: Inflation Risk
definition: Inflation risk is the danger that the purchasing power of money will decline due to rising prices, eroding real investment returns.
example: If inflation is 4% while a savings account yields 2%, the real return is negative 2%.

title: Credit Risk
definition: Credit risk is the risk that a borrower will default on a loan or bond, failing to make required interest or principal payments. Higher credit risk demands higher returns to compensate investors.
example: A bond issued by a company with a low credit rating carries greater credit risk and must offer a higher yield.

title: Liquidity Risk
definition: Liquidity risk is the risk that an investor or company will be unable to quickly buy or sell an asset without significantly affecting its price.
example: Real estate typically has higher liquidity risk than publicly traded stocks because it may take months to sell property at fair value.

title: Market Risk Premium
definition: The market risk premium is the additional return investors require for choosing a risky market portfolio over a risk-free investment. It equals the difference between the expected market return and the risk-free rate.
example: If the expected market return is 8% and the risk-free rate is 3%, the market risk premium is 5%.

title: Equity Risk Premium
definition: The equity risk premium is the excess return that investing in the stock market provides over a risk-free rate. It compensates investors for the additional risk of equities.
example: If long-term government bonds yield 2% and the stock market is expected to return 7%, the equity risk premium is 5%.

title: Effective Annual Rate (EAR)
definition: The effective annual rate is the actual annual rate of interest earned or paid on an investment or loan after accounting for compounding within the year.
example: A nominal rate of 12% compounded monthly results in an EAR of (1 + 0.12/12)^12 – 1 ≈ 12.68%.

title: Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR)
definition: The compound annual growth rate is the annualized rate of return that equalizes the beginning and ending values of an investment over a specified period, assuming the investment grows at a constant rate.
example: An investment that grows from $10,000 to $16,000 over 5 years has a CAGR of (16,000 ÷ 10,000)^(1/5) – 1 ≈ 9.86%.

title: Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR)
definition: The modified internal rate of return adjusts the internal rate of return by assuming that positive cash flows are reinvested at the project’s cost of capital and that initial outlays are financed at the financing rate. It provides a more realistic measure of investment returns.
example: A project with an MIRR of 12% and a cost of capital of 10% is considered acceptable because it exceeds the hurdle rate.

title: Profitability Index (PI)
definition: The profitability index is the ratio of the present value of future cash flows to the initial investment. A PI greater than 1 indicates that the project generates value and should be accepted.
example: If the present value of a project’s inflows is $1.2 million and the initial cost is $1 million, the profitability index is 1.2.

title: Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)
definition: The capital asset pricing model estimates the expected return of an asset based on its beta and the market risk premium: Expected Return = Risk-free rate + Beta × (Market return – Risk-free rate).
example: For a stock with a beta of 1.5, a risk-free rate of 2%, and a market risk premium of 4%, the expected return is 2% + 1.5 × 4% = 8%.

title: Treynor Ratio
definition: The Treynor ratio measures the returns earned in excess of the risk-free rate per unit of market risk, as measured by beta. It is calculated as (Portfolio return – Risk-free rate) ÷ Beta.
example: A portfolio that returns 12%, with a risk-free rate of 3% and beta of 1.2, has a Treynor ratio of (12 – 3) ÷ 1.2 = 7.5%.

title: Sortino Ratio
definition: The Sortino ratio is a variation of the Sharpe ratio that uses downside deviation instead of standard deviation to measure risk. It focuses on negative volatility and is calculated as (Portfolio return – Risk-free rate) ÷ Downside deviation.
example: A fund with a return of 10%, risk-free rate of 2%, and downside deviation of 5% has a Sortino ratio of (10 – 2) ÷ 5 = 1.6.

title: Information Ratio
definition: The information ratio compares a portfolio’s active return (return above the benchmark) to the variability of that active return (tracking error). A higher ratio indicates better risk-adjusted performance.
example: A portfolio’s active return of 2% and tracking error of 1% results in an information ratio of 2.

title: Dividend Discount Model (DDM)
definition: The dividend discount model values a stock by estimating the present value of its expected future dividends, discounted back to today at the required rate of return.
example: A stock that pays an annual dividend of $2 expected to grow at 5% indefinitely, with a required return of 10%, has a DDM value of $2 ÷ (0.10 – 0.05) = $40.

title: Gordon Growth Model (GGM)
definition: The Gordon Growth Model is a version of the DDM that assumes dividends will grow at a constant rate forever. The stock’s value equals next year’s dividend divided by the difference between required return and growth rate.
example: Using the GGM, a dividend of $2 with 5% growth and a 10% required return yields a value of $2 ÷ (0.10 – 0.05) = $40.

title: Price-to-Free-Cash-Flow Ratio
definition: The price-to-free-cash-flow ratio divides a company’s market capitalization by its free cash flow. It indicates how much investors are willing to pay per dollar of free cash flow.
example: A company with a market cap of $500 M and free cash flow of $50 M has a P/FCF ratio of 10.

title: Enterprise Value to EBITDA (EV/EBITDA) Ratio
definition: The EV/EBITDA ratio compares a company’s enterprise value to its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. A lower ratio may suggest a company is undervalued.
example: If a company has an EV of $600 M and an EBITDA of $120 M, its EV/EBITDA ratio is 5.

title: Earnings Before Interest and Taxes (EBIT)
definition: Earnings before interest and taxes, also called operating income, is a company’s profit after deducting operating expenses but before subtracting interest and taxes.
example: A firm with revenue of $2 M, cost of goods sold of $1 M, and operating expenses of $350 K has an EBIT of $650 K.

title: Earnings Before Taxes (EBT)
definition: Earnings before taxes is a company’s income after deducting operating expenses and interest expenses but before taxes. It is calculated by subtracting interest expense from EBIT.
example: If a company reports EBIT of $650 K and interest expenses of $100 K, its EBT is $550 K.

title: Total Return
definition: Total return measures the overall return on an investment, combining capital appreciation and income (dividends or interest). It is expressed as a percentage of the initial investment.
example: A stock’s price rises 10% and it pays a 2% dividend over a year, giving a total return of 12%.

title: Risk-Adjusted Return
definition: Risk-adjusted return evaluates the return of an investment relative to the amount of risk taken. Metrics like the Sharpe, Treynor, and Sortino ratios adjust returns for volatility or downside risk.
example: Two funds each return 8%, but the one with lower volatility has a higher risk-adjusted return as measured by the Sharpe ratio.

title: Option Greek Delta
definition: Delta measures the sensitivity of an option’s price to a $1 change in the price of the underlying asset. A call option’s delta ranges between 0 and 1, while a put option’s delta ranges between -1 and 0.
example: A call option with a delta of 0.6 will increase approximately $0.60 if the underlying stock price rises by $1.

title: Option Greek Gamma
definition: Gamma measures the rate of change of an option’s delta with respect to changes in the underlying asset’s price. A high gamma indicates the option’s delta is very sensitive to price changes.
example: If an option’s delta increases from 0.6 to 0.7 when the underlying price rises by $1, the gamma is 0.1.

title: Option Greek Vega
definition: Vega measures the sensitivity of an option’s price to changes in the volatility of the underlying asset. It indicates how much the option’s value will change for a 1% change in implied volatility.
example: An option with a vega of 0.05 will increase by $0.05 if implied volatility rises by 1%.

title: Option Greek Theta
definition: Theta measures the rate at which an option’s price declines due to the passage of time, often called time decay. A negative theta indicates that the option loses value each day all else equal.
example: A call option with a theta of -0.02 will lose about $0.02 in value per day, assuming other factors remain constant.

title: Volatility
definition: Volatility represents the degree of variation of a trading price series over time. It is typically measured by the standard deviation or variance of returns and reflects the risk associated with an asset.
example: A stock with frequent large price swings has higher volatility than a stock with relatively stable prices.

title: Yield Spread
definition: Yield spread is the difference between the yields of two debt instruments, often of different credit qualities or maturities. It helps investors compare the relative risk and return of bonds.
example: A 10-year corporate bond yields 5% while a 10-year Treasury bond yields 3%; the yield spread is 2%.

title: Credit Spread
definition: Credit spread is the difference in yield between a corporate bond and a comparable risk-free government bond, reflecting the additional compensation required for bearing credit risk.
example: If a corporate bond yields 4.5% and a risk-free government bond yields 2%, the credit spread is 2.5%.

title: Mortgage-Backed Security (MBS)
definition: A mortgage-backed security is an investment backed by a pool of mortgages. Investors receive periodic payments derived from the principal and interest on the underlying mortgages.
example: A bank bundles home mortgages and sells them to investors as MBS, who then receive monthly payments from the mortgage borrowers.

title: Collateralized Debt Obligation (CDO)
definition: A collateralized debt obligation is a complex financial product backed by a pool of loans and other assets. It is divided into tranches with varying risk and return levels, allowing investors to select their preferred risk profile.
example: A CDO may bundle corporate loans, mortgages, and other debt instruments. Senior tranches have priority in receiving payments but offer lower yields compared to subordinate tranches.

title: Option Greek Rho
definition: Rho measures the sensitivity of an option’s price to changes in the risk-free interest rate. A positive rho means that a rise in interest rates will increase the value of a call option and decrease the value of a put option.
example: A call option with rho of 0.04 will gain about $0.04 if interest rates rise by 1%.
